scenes: June fourth, nineteen forty two. The middle of the Pacific Ocean.
June 4, 1942. The middle of the Pacific Ocean.
It is twenty past ten in the morning, and a Japanese admiral is standing on the bridge of his flagship.
Around him are four aircraft carriers. The same four that helped bomb Pearl Harbor.
For three hours, American planes have been attacking them.
Wave after wave.
And not one bomb, not one torpedo, has hit.
He is winning.
In about five minutes... three of those four carriers will be on fire.
For six months after Pearl Harbor, Japan won almost everywhere it went.
But the admiral who planned that attack knew he had missed something.
The American aircraft carriers had not been in port that day.
And as long as they were afloat, the job was not finished.
His name was Yamamoto. And he had a plan to draw them out.
He would attack a speck of an island called Midway, thirteen hundred miles from Hawaii.
He would attack a speck of an island called Midway, 1,300 miles from Hawaii.
The Americans would have to come out and defend it.
And when they did, his carriers would be waiting.
What Yamamoto did not know was that somebody was reading his mail.
In a basement at Pearl Harbor, a team of Navy codebreakers had been taking apart the Japanese naval code, piece by piece.
Their boss was a commander named Joseph Roashfort.
Their boss was a commander named Joseph Rochefort.
They could read enough to know a big attack was coming.
And they knew the target, by its code name. Two letters.
A. F.
Roashfort was sure A. F. meant Midway. Washington was not.
Rochefort was sure A. F. meant Midway. Washington was not.
So they set a trap.
Midway was told to radio, in plain English, that its fresh water plant had broken down.
Within a day, the codebreakers picked up a Japanese message.
A. F. is short of water.
Now the American commander, Admiral Chester Nimitz, knew where, and he knew about when.
What he did not have was ships.
He had two carriers ready. A third, the Yorktown, had just limped home from battle with a bomb hole through her decks.
The repair yard figured she needed months.
Nimitz gave them three days.
She sailed with repair crews still working on board.
Three American carriers slipped out, and waited north of Midway.
The men setting the ambush... were about to walk into one.
At four thirty on the morning of June fourth, the Japanese carriers turned into the wind.
At 4:30 on the morning of June 4, the Japanese carriers turned into the wind.
The man in command of them was Admiral Nahgoomo.
The man in command of them was Admiral Nagumo.
He sent a hundred and eight planes to bomb Midway.
He sent 108 planes to bomb Midway.
They hit it hard. But the airfield was still working, and the strike leader radioed back.
There is need for a second attack.
Nahgoomo had a second wave ready. But it was armed with torpedoes, to sink ships.
Nagumo had a second wave ready. But it was armed with torpedoes, to sink ships.
And as far as he knew, there were no ships.
So he gave the order. Take off the torpedoes. Load bombs.
Below decks, the crews got to work.
Then a scout plane, one that had taken off half an hour late, sent a message.
Ten ships. To the east.
And a little later... one of them looks like a carrier.
Nahgoomo reversed his order. Take off the bombs. Put the torpedoes back.
Nagumo reversed his order. Take off the bombs. Put the torpedoes back.
There was no time to put anything away.
Bombs were stacked in the hangars. Fuel hoses ran across the decks.
And now his first wave was coming home from Midway, low on gas, needing somewhere to land.
He could launch what he had right now, or he could land his planes, arm everything, and hit the Americans with one clean blow.
He decided to wait.
All that time, the Americans kept coming.
First from Midway itself. Marine pilots. Army bombers. Six brand new torpedo planes.
Most of them were shot down, and nothing hit.
Then came the planes from the carriers.
The torpedo bombers found the Japanese first.
They were slow, they were old, and most of them had no fighter cover.
To drop a torpedo, they had to fly low and straight, right into the guns.
Torpedo Squadron Eight went in with fifteen planes.
All fifteen were shot down.
Of thirty men, one lived. A young pilot named George Gay, who floated in the wreckage all day, and watched.
Two more squadrons followed them in.
Forty one torpedo planes attacked that morning.
Thirty four did not come back.
Not one torpedo hit.
But they had done something, without knowing it.
They had pulled the Japanese fighters down to the water, and kept the carriers dodging, too busy to launch.
And high above, there was one more group of Americans. Dive bombers, from the carrier Enterprise.
Their leader was a man named Wade McClusky.
He had flown to the spot where the Japanese were supposed to be.
There was nothing there but ocean.
His planes were running low on fuel. Going on meant some of them would not make it home.
He went on.
And then he saw a wake. One Japanese destroyer, alone, running north in a hurry.
It had stayed behind to chase off an American submarine, and now it was racing to catch up with its fleet.
McClusky followed it.
At ten twenty two, the dive bombers rolled over, and came straight down.
At 10:22, the dive bombers rolled over, and came straight down.
There were no fighters up high to stop them.
The carrier Kahga took four bombs, or more.
The carrier Kaga took four bombs, or more.
The flagship, Akagi, took one.
It went through the deck, into a hangar full of fueled planes, and bombs that nobody had put away.
And at that same moment, by pure chance, a second group of dive bombers arrived from a different direction.
They were from the Yorktown. The ship that was supposed to be in dry dock.
They put three bombs into a third carrier, the Soreyoo.
They put three bombs into a third carrier, the Soryu.
By ten twenty six, all three were burning from end to end.
By 10:26, all three were burning from end to end.
Twenty minutes later, Nahgoomo abandoned his flagship.
Twenty minutes later, Nagumo abandoned his flagship.
It had taken about five minutes.
There was one Japanese carrier left. The Heeryoo.
There was one Japanese carrier left. The Hiryu.
She struck back. Her planes followed the Americans home, and hit the Yorktown with three bombs.
The crew patched the deck and got her moving again, so fast, that when the second wave arrived, they thought they were attacking a different ship.
They hit her again, with torpedoes. This time, she stopped.
But that afternoon, American scouts found the Heeryoo.
But that afternoon, American scouts found the Hiryu.
At five o'clock, the dive bombers came down one more time.
Four hits.
Yamamoto was hundreds of miles behind, with his battleships. He had nothing left to fight with.
He turned the fleet around, and went home.
Japan lost four aircraft carriers, a heavy cruiser, and about two hundred and fifty planes.
Japan lost four aircraft carriers, a heavy cruiser, and about 250 planes.
More than three thousand men.
More than 3,000 men.
The United States lost one carrier, the Yorktown, one destroyer, and about a hundred and fifty planes.

307 men.
In Japan, the newspapers were told it was a great victory.
The wounded were kept away from their families, so nobody would talk.
The war went on for three more years.
But after Midway, Japan never had the upper hand at sea again.
And it turned on small things.
A code, half broken. A ship, fixed in three days.
Men in old planes, who flew in knowing what would happen.
And one pilot, who should have turned back...
and kept looking.
